plan.title: Toy car loop-the-loop
physics: rigid-body dynamics of the car along the track (Newton's second law along the path)
unilateral contact: normal force N = m (v^2 kappa + g cos theta) >= 0
rolling resistance C_rr N and aerodynamic drag 0.5 rho C_d A v^2
clothoid (Euler spiral) entry and exit: curvature rising linearly to 1/R
track strip in bending under the peak contact load (simply supported between stand clamps)
assumptions: the car is a point on its centre-of-mass path for the 1-D model; Newton models it as a rigid sphere of the wheel radius
rolling losses are lumped into one coefficient C_rr = force / normal force
wheels: four solid PLA discs, their rotation adds inertia (not weight)
air at 20 °C, 1 atm (density from the ideal gas law)
the track is rigid and does not move (clamped to its stands)

verification.label: Newton rigid-body contact

checks.name: car stays on the track and reaches the end (both time steps)
checks.detail: largest gap between the car and the running surface in the loop [m]; the car must not leave the track before the end of the run-out

checks.name: speed at the top insensitive to the time step
Newton within 10 % of the 1-D model without losses
checks.detail: v_top 1.507 (Newton, frictionless) vs 1.617 m/s (1-D, no friction, no air): the gap is the contact's numerical dissipation

checks.name: Newton Coulomb friction (analytic sliding case)
checks.detail: stopping distance [m]: 0.5087 vs 0.5097 on a flat surface

notes: NVIDIA Newton 1.7.0, XPBD, 12 iterations: the car is a sphere of the wheel radius (6 mm) on the 3-D track mesh (strip, rails, the exit shifted sideways), launched at the design speed; no air

Newton loses 5.7 % of the launch energy by the top with no friction at all: XPBD contact dissipation on the curved mesh, which barely changes with the time step or a finer mesh. The run is therefore judged against the worst-case envelope (it must still go round and keep at least the envelope's speed at the top), not for equality.

Friction is not used in the loop run: Newton's Coulomb friction is checked on its analytic flat sliding case, but on the curved track mesh a rolling sphere with friction loses most of its energy (measured while building this template), so the rolling-resistance envelope stays in the 1-D model.

build_instructions: Measure the car's rolling resistance first: on a straight strip of the track material tilted by an angle a, find the smallest angle at which the car keeps rolling at constant speed; C_rr = tan(a). This design completes the loop for C_rr up to 0.0695.
Print or cut the track strip (PLA (Ingeo 4043D), 1.5 mm thick) from track.stl / track.step: 134 cm of running surface, 40 mm wide, with 8 mm side rails.
Shape the loop: top arc radius 8.4 cm, entry and exit clothoids 21.0 cm long; the exit is shifted 5 cm sideways so it clears the entry.
Clamp the strip to a stand every 10 cm; the loop is 18.8 cm tall.
Set the launcher to 2.47 m/s (+-5 %); check with a phone slow-motion video over the 30 cm run-in.
First runs: start 10 % below the design speed and raise it until the car completes the loop; the operating window table gives the speed range that works.
limits: The car is a point on its centre-of-mass path (1-D model) or a sphere (Newton); wheel bounce, steering and track joints are not modelled.
Newton's check has no friction and no air, and its contact dissipates energy: it confirms the 3-D track lets the car go round with margin, not the 1-D model's speeds to a tolerance.
Rolling resistance and drag are envelopes, not measurements: the design covers them, a car outside them (bent axle, dirty wheels) may not complete the loop.
The track strength check is a beam under a point load between clamps; the clamps, the stand and fatigue of the strip are not checked.
Toy scale only: nothing here applies to rides that carry people.

savings.text: 8600 design evaluations ran on the closed form and the reduced model; the full solver ran 1 time(s) at 272.5 s each (measured). Running every evaluation on the full solver would have taken about 651.1 h (estimate: evaluations x measured time per full call).
